name: Tiji
image_query: Tiji festival Lo Manthang masked dance
when: Three days in the third Tibetan month, usually May (14–16 May in 2026)
summary: Tiji is Lo Manthang's great three-day festival, held each May in the square before the old royal palace. Monks of Chhoede gompa perform masked dances that tell how the deity Dorje Jono defeated a demon who brought drought and suffering to Lo, purifying the land for the year ahead.
body: Tiji is the most important festival of Upper Mustang. It is held over three days in the third month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in May; in 2026 it ran from 14 to 16 May. The lamas of Chhoede gompa, the main working monastery of Lo Manthang, set the dates each year. Families from across Lo arrive in the walled city in their finest clothes and jewellery, and every rooftop around the palace square fills with spectators.

The dances tell a legend. A demon born in Lo brought drought, disease and misfortune to the land, and the deity Dorje Jono took on the task of defeating him. Over three days, masked monks in brocade costumes dance the story to the sound of long horns, drums and cymbals. Each day has its own dances, building to the final day, when the demon's effigy is destroyed and Lo is purified for the coming year.

Under the kingdom, the king of Lo presided over Tiji from the palace. Since the end of the monarchy in 2008, the festival has carried on, and members of the former royal family still attend. For visitors, Tiji is the busiest and most rewarding time to be in Lo Manthang. Lodges are booked months ahead, and the restricted area permit and flights to Jomsom need early planning.
tips: Arrive in Lo Manthang at least a day before Tiji begins to acclimatise at 3,840 m.
Find your place in the palace square early each morning and bring a cushion, sun hat and warm layers.
Never step into the dance area, keep flash off and follow the stewards' instructions.

faqs.a: Tiji is held over three days in the third month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in May. In 2026 it took place on 14–16 May. The dates are set each year by the lamas of Chhoede gompa in Lo Manthang, so they move against the Western calendar. Check current dates before you travel and book early.

Monks of Chhoede gompa perform masked dances in the palace square of Lo Manthang over three days. The dances tell the legend of Dorje Jono, who defeats a demon that brought drought and suffering to Lo. On the final day the demon's effigy is destroyed, symbolising the purification of the land for the year ahead.

faqs.q: How do I get to Tiji in Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: Fly Pokhara–Jomsom, then drive 6–7 hours by jeep or trek 4–5 days from Kagbeni to Lo Manthang. You need an Upper Mustang restricted area permit, arranged through a registered agency for at least two people with a licensed guide. Plan at least 10 days from Pokhara, with spare days for flights.

By Mustang standards, yes. Lo Manthang's lodges fill up, and the palace square is packed with local families, monks and visitors, especially on the second and third days. It is still small compared with festivals in Kathmandu. Book lodges and permits four to six months ahead, and arrive early each morning for a good spot.

name: Yartung
when: Around the full moon of Janai Purnima, usually August or early September
summary: Yartung, from the Tibetan for 'end of summer', is a three-day festival held around the full moon of August at Muktinath and in Lo Manthang. Villagers of Baragaun and Lo gather for horse races, archery, dancing and drinking, with riders in their best clothes racing across the meadows below the temple.
body: Yartung marks the end of summer in Mustang, before the harvest and the move to winter. The name is usually explained from Tibetan: yar, summer, and tung, end. It is held around the full moon of the Nepali month of Shrawan, the same full moon that Hindus celebrate as Janai Purnima, which usually falls in August. The best-known celebrations are at Muktinath and in Lo Manthang, though villages across Mustang mark it.

At Muktinath, families from Ranipauwa, Jharkot, Kagbeni and the other Baragaun villages gather on the meadows below the temple. The heart of the festival is horse racing: men and women ride decorated horses at full speed across the open ground, watched by crowds on the slopes. There are archery contests, dancing, songs and plenty of chhang and rakshi. Lamas also perform rituals for the community.

Because Janai Purnima falls at the same time, Hindu pilgrims are often at Muktinath too, bathing under the 108 spouts and tying the sacred thread, so Yartung shows Muktinath's two faiths side by side. August is in the monsoon, which brings little rain to Mustang but often disrupts flights to Jomsom and the road from Beni, so allow plenty of spare time.
tips: Check the exact dates with local contacts before you plan; they follow the lunar calendar.
Watch the horse races from the slopes, well back from the course, as riders go at full speed.
Keep two spare days in your plan for monsoon disruption to Jomsom flights and the Beni road.

faqs.a: Yartung is held around the full moon of Janai Purnima, which usually falls in August, sometimes early September. It lasts about three days. Exact dates follow the lunar calendar and are confirmed locally each year, so check current dates before you travel. Celebrations at Muktinath and Lo Manthang may differ slightly in timing.

Yartung celebrates the end of summer with horse races, archery, dancing, singing and feasting. Riders in their best clothes race decorated horses across the meadows, and families gather from villages across the area. Lamas perform rituals for the community. At Muktinath, Hindu pilgrims are often present for Janai Purnima at the same time.

faqs.q: Do I need a special permit for Yartung at Muktinath?
faqs.a: No restricted area permit is needed for Muktinath; an ACAP permit and TIMS card are enough, and since April 2023 a licensed guide in conservation areas. If you want to see Yartung in Lo Manthang, you need an Upper Mustang restricted area permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit Mustang?
faqs.a: Mustang lies in the rain shadow, so August is mostly dry there, with green fields and few visitors. The problem is getting in: monsoon cloud often delays Pokhara–Jomsom flights, and landslides can close the road between Beni and Ghasa. Allow spare days and travel with a flexible plan.

name: Shey festival (Shey Mela)
when: Once every 12 years, in the Tibetan year of the Dragon, around August–September (last held 2024; next expected 2036)
summary: The Shey festival is held only once every 12 years, in the Tibetan year of the Dragon, at Shey Gompa, the Crystal Monastery of Upper Dolpo. Pilgrims walk around the Crystal Mountain, lamas give teachings, and there are horse races and archery. The last was in 2024; the next is expected in 2036.
body: Shey Gompa, the Crystal Monastery, stands at about 4,200 m in Upper Dolpo, north of Phoksundo Lake. Founded in the 11th century, it is regarded as the spiritual heart of Upper Dolpo, and the Crystal Mountain above it is a sacred peak for the people of the region. Once every twelve years, in the Tibetan year of the Dragon, a great festival is held here. It took place in 2012 and in 2024, and the next is expected in 2036.

During the festival, pilgrims from across Dolpo and beyond walk the kora, the circuit around the Crystal Mountain, a long walk at high altitude. Lamas give teachings and blessings, and there are cultural performances, horse races and archery contests. Local tradition links the festival's origins to a victory over evil spirits. It was at Shey that Peter Matthiessen and George Schaller arrived in 1973, the journey told in The Snow Leopard.

Reaching Shey is a serious undertaking. From Phoksundo Lake, the route runs along the lake's western shore and crosses the Kang La, at over 5,300 m, taking 3–4 days. It lies in Upper Dolpo, which requires its own restricted area permit, a licensed guide and a fully supported camping trek. Outside festival years, Shey can still be visited on Upper Dolpo treks, usually in May–June and September–October.
tips: Plan years ahead for the next festival, expected in 2036, and confirm the exact dates locally.
Allow at least three weeks from Kathmandu for a trek to Shey via Juphal and Phoksundo Lake.
Arrive acclimatised: Shey is at about 4,200 m and the kora goes higher.

faqs.q: How often is the Shey festival held?
faqs.a: The Shey festival is held once every 12 years, in the Tibetan year of the Dragon, at Shey Gompa in Upper Dolpo. It took place in 2012 and in 2024, and the next is expected in 2036. Exact dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and are confirmed nearer the time; check current status before you travel.

Shey Gompa, the Crystal Monastery, is in Upper Dolpo in Dolpa district, at about 4,200 m, north of Phoksundo Lake in Shey Phoksundo National Park. It is reached in 3–4 days from Ringmo via the western shore of the lake and the Kang La pass, over 5,300 m. It was founded in the 11th century.

faqs.q: What permit do I need for the Shey festival?
faqs.a: Shey lies in Upper Dolpo, which needs a restricted area permit, as we understand it USD 500 per person for the first 10 days and USD 50 per day after, plus a Shey Phoksundo National Park permit. The permit is issued through a registered agency for at least two trekkers with a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Shey Gompa outside the festival year?
faqs.a: Yes. Shey Gompa can be visited on Upper Dolpo treks in any season when the passes are open, usually May–June and September–October. You will see the monastery and the Crystal Mountain, and may be able to walk the kora with a guide, but without the crowds, teachings and games of the 12-yearly festival.
